chapters.title: Chapter 5 · The Fox Who Played Dead
chapters.artPrompt: a red fox lying stiff on its back in the middle of a dusty country road with one eye slyly half-open, a grey-brown rabbit standing a careful distance away with ears up, long pine shadows across the lane, warm late-afternoon light, comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Brer Fox had not given up on catching Brer Rabbit — not by a long sight. One morning he lay down flat in the middle of the big road, stiff as a fence rail, and played dead.
"There," said Brer Fox to himself, "when Brer Rabbit comes by, he will come close to look. And then I will have him at last."

By and by Brer Rabbit came hopping down the road, and there lay Brer Fox. Brer Rabbit stopped, and looked, and thought. "That looks mighty like Brer Fox," he said. "But I heard he was dead. And in this country, dead folks always keep their eyes wide open."
Brer Rabbit looks closely at the fox lying flat in the road.

Quicker than a wink, Brer Fox's eyes snapped shut. Then he knew he had given himself away! Brer Rabbit laughed till he had to hold his sides. "You may fool the crows, Brer Fox," he called over his shoulder, "but you can't fool me!"
And away he went down the road, singing at the top of his voice, while the fox lay in the dust feeling smaller than a striped snake.
Ask your child: is the fox really dead? How does Brer Rabbit find out? Talk about staying calm and watching closely before you believe something.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Fate of Mr. Jack Sparrow
chapters.artPrompt: a rabbit caught in a woven snare at the edge of a thicket looking up with a sly smile, a jaunty little sparrow perched on a black walnut branch above leaning down to tease, dappled woodland light, comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: One day Brer Rabbit hopped where he had no business hopping, and smack! He was caught in a snare that Brer Fox had fixed in the thicket. He pulled and twisted, but the snare held fast.
Up on a black walnut branch sat Mr. Jack Sparrow, and when he saw Brer Rabbit caught, he could not hold his tongue. "Caught at last, Brer Rabbit!" he chirped. "Who is smart now? Ha-ha!"
Mr. Jack Sparrow leans from the branch, teasing, while the snare holds Brer Rabbit.
Brer Rabbit did not get angry. He got thinking. "Don't tease me, friend," he said sadly. "And do come down close, for I can't hear a word you say."

Down fluttered Mr. Jack Sparrow, wanting to hear himself laugh again. He hopped a step nearer. Then another. And quick as a flash, Brer Rabbit had him — swallow, and it was all over, feathers and all. And that was the fate of Mr. Jack Sparrow.

Then Brer Rabbit carried the chattering bird back to the very branch where the teasing had started. "Now remember," he said, kindly enough, "a good neighbor laughs with you, not at you." And he set Mr. Jack Sparrow free, wiser by one afternoon.
Brer Rabbit, who knew every trick of every snare in the county, soon slipped loose and hopped home singing. And no bird ever teased Brer Rabbit again.
Ask your child: Jack Sparrow was only joking — but was it kind? What could he have done instead of teasing?

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Mr. Rabbit Nibbles up the Butter
chapters.artPrompt: a log cabin storeroom at night where a rabbit in a nightcap dips a paw into a round ball of butter on a high shelf, a candle stub burning low, warm mischievous shadows, comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Brer Fox, Brer Wolf, Brer Rabbit and Brer Bear laid in a great round ball of butter for the winter, and they kept it in a corner of Brer Fox's storeroom, all agreed and done fair.

Now Brer Rabbit loved butter better than his own tail. Every few nights he would say, "My sister's taken sick — mind the house while I'm gone!" And off he would slip through the moonlight. And nibble, nibble, nibble went Brer Rabbit at the butter.
By and by Brer Fox measured the butter ball and found it shrinking small. The friends all met together, and nobody would own up to it.
The four friends sit around the shrunken butter ball, each eyeing the others.

"I know a test," said Brer Rabbit sweetly. "The one who ate the butter will smell of it. Let us sleep by the fire, and the butter will show on us." Late that night he crept about in the dark, and smeared butter, soft and gold, all around Brer Fox's sleeping mouth.
In the morning there was Brer Fox, smelling of butter from whiskers to ears! Nobody would hear a word he said. And Brer Rabbit sat in the corner looking as innocent as Sunday.
New word: own up — to tell the truth about something you did. Ask your child: who really ate the butter? What should Brer Rabbit have done when the butter was missed?

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Awful Fate of Mr. Wolf
chapters.artPrompt: a long grey wolf sticking his head into a dark hollow tree trunk while a golden cloud of bees boils out around his ears, a rabbit peeking from behind a pine at the clearing's edge, dramatic late sunlight, comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: After his many failures, Brer Wolf grew sadder and sadder, and hungrier and hungrier, till at last he caught Brer Rabbit in a narrow gully between two hills.
"Now," said Brer Wolf, "there is no river to cross and no briars to run to. I have you."

Brer Rabbit looked at him with big, sad eyes. "Very well, Brer Wolf," he said meekly. "But before you eat me, look at this hollow tree. It is the finest horse stable in the county, and my folks keep their racing horses there. Peek in and count them, and then do as you please."
Brer Wolf peeps into the hollow tree — just as the golden cloud comes out.

Brer Wolf put his eye to the hole in the tree. "I don't see any horses—" he began. But what he saw was a whir and a golden cloud. For the hollow tree was full of wild bees, and every bee came out mad as a hornet's nest in church.

They stung him on the ears, the nose, the tail and the toes. Brer Wolf howled down the gully and off through the woods, swollen like a feed sack, and he never troubled Brer Rabbit's side of the county again. And Brer Rabbit dusted off his paws and went home to supper.
Ask your child: Brer Rabbit could not run this time. What did he do instead of fighting? Talk about using your wits when your legs are not enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Why Mr. Possum Loves Peace
chapters.artPrompt: a small grey possum with a pink nose lying flat on the ground and grinning up at a puzzled rabbit, a persimmon grove in silvery moonlight, fallen persimmons dotting the grass, funny gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: Brer Rabbit was always quarreling with somebody — with Brer Fox, with Brer Wolf, with Brer Bear. So he was mightily puzzled by Mr. Possum, who never quarreled with anybody at all.
"How do you keep out of all the fights?" Brer Rabbit asked him. "I am a man of peace," said Mr. Possum, smiling a slow, sweet smile. Brer Rabbit laughed inside his sleeve, but he said nothing.
Mr. Possum smiles his slow smile while Brer Rabbit watches, curious.

One moonshiny night the hounds came baying through the persimmon grove, and Brer Rabbit ran for his life. When the noise died away, he crept back — and there lay Mr. Possum flat on the ground, still as a dropped persimmon.
The hounds sniffed him and poked him, but Mr. Possum never so much as wiggled a whisker. At last the hounds trotted off whining, for they could not raise a game.

Then one eye of Mr. Possum twinkled up at Brer Rabbit, and he picked himself up, grinning from ear to ear. "You see, Brer Rabbit," he said, "this is how I love my peace. I let the quarrels pass me by, and play I am nobody at all." And Brer Rabbit laughed till morning.
New word: quarrel — a loud argument between friends. Ask your child: what is Mr. Possum's secret trick? Is staying out of a quarrel ever the smartest move?
